articles.title_orig: The struggle over what China wants
articles.title_zh: The struggle over what China wants
articles.content_orig:
Peer reviewed analysis from world leading experts
The University of Technology Sydney
China expertise is itself a field of epistemic struggle, shaped by competing convictions, dispositions and geopolitical perspectives. Doshi’s critique of Kang, Wong and Chan’s analysis that China is not a revisionist power is methodological in nature, but differing threat perceptions among policymakers and experts suggest that geopolitics determines whose view prevails. Expert consensus on what China wants, then, is unlikely to emerge anytime soon. To advance the quest to gauge what China wants, scholars need to examine not only the evidence about China but also the power dynamics through which knowledge about China is produced.
The current debate on the question of what China wants shows no sign of reaching a consensus. Some may be of the impression that agreement is possible so long as methodological differences can be resolved, yet few acknowledge that the fault line in the debate is epistemological rather than methodological.
In August 2025, Dave Kang, Jackie Wong and Zenobia Chan published a peer-reviewed article in International Security titled ‘ What Does China Want? ’, which concluded that China is a status quo power with limited global aims, not a revisionist state seeking to dramatically expand its power and reshape the world order.
The paper has generated significant debate. In August 2025, the same journal published four critical responses , all focusing on methodological issues. The most developed critique is from former Biden administration senior policy advisor Rush Doshi. His 2021 book, The Long Game , came to the opposite conclusion: that Beijing has pursued a long-term strategy to displace US influence regionally and globally.
This raises the question of what methodology could reliably establish China’s intentions. Kang, Wong and Chan evaluate intent through a large-scale analysis of 12,000 official Chinese articles, supplemented by a qualitative reading of hundreds of Xi Jinping’s speeches. But Doshi argues that the authors draw the wrong conclusions by ‘cherry-picking’ from an overly narrow selection of Chinese sources and ‘treating the resultant absence of evidence as the evidence of absence’. His own approach examines China’s actions alongside textual evidence, drawing on a more curated selection of official and unofficial sources.
Yet a consistent and rigorous triangulation would require not only analysing official and internal statements, elite writings, policy decisions and actual behaviour, but also examining these decisions against alternative courses of action and tracing the changes over time. Neither critique seems to fully meet this benchmark.
Beyond methodology, the debate also exposes the disciplinary limitations of international relations and political science. Understanding intent is as much a psychological process as it is an analytical one, involving emotion as well as reasoning. Robert Jervis famously examined the role of psychology in shaping US misperceptions of the Soviet Union’s malign intentions during the Cold War. In other words, to get closer to knowing an adversary’s intentions, there must be an analytical mechanism capable of dealing with emotions such as anxiety and fear.
The third question is whether China’s intentions can be meaningfully evaluated at all in a political climate shaped by mutual distrust. While Kang, Wong and Chan reached their conclusion that China does not intend to become a global hegemon after analysing 12,000 articles and speeches, sceptics may argue that Beijing is simply concealing its intentions — a claim that no amount of empirical evidence can disprove.
The easiest way out of this cognitive conundrum could be to simply equate capacity with intention, but this would be dangerous. Capability tells us what a state can do, not necessarily what it wants to do. China’s capabilities are real — its nuclear arsenal is growing, its navy is enormous; and Beijing’s military spending is substantial. But a country can acquire capabilities for several reasons, including deterrence, concerns about an adversary’s capabilities, the need to project might to its domestic public, competing bureaucratic interests and a perceived need to shore up security against an uncertain future.
This raises the difficult question of whether changing capabilities may lead to a change in intention. Doshi argues that China’s growing capabilities have changed its operational tempo and increased its risk tolerance, and that its behaviour, such as clashes with neighbours, should be incorporated into assessments of its intentions.
The epistemological challenge of gauging China’s intentions has taken on added urgency under intensifying US–China rivalry . As one commentator remarks, the question of ‘what does China want’ has become so perennial that it is now a ‘ genre unto itself ’. Perhaps the main value of Kang, Wong and Chan’s paper lies in reopening a debate that may have been prematurely treated as settled.
The debate reveals a deeper institutional tension. A March 2026 study found that US policymakers are far more likely to view China as a threat than think tank researchers, academics and the public. One possible explanation could be that academics and researchers seeking scholarly credibility are concerned with producing reliable and falsifiable evidence about China’s intentions, whereas policymakers align more closely with the political values, ideological commitments and institutional interests of powerful elites.
The same study finds that among researchers and academics, self-identified security experts have a higher threat perception of China than self-identified East Asia experts. This epistemological divide cannot be resolved by methodological rigour. Instead, we should go beyond methodology to examine how geopolitics shapes knowledge production and how these power dynamics in turn determine which approach prevails in answering the question of what China really wants.
And above all, we should acknowledge, as David McCourt, a sociologist of knowledge production, argues , that China expertise is always a field of ‘intense struggle’ over expertise, and that how we come to know China depends as much on our own professional ‘convictions’ and ‘institutional dispositions’ as on how we respond to the ‘objective distributions in the balance of international power’.
Wanning Sun is Professor of Media and Communication Studies at University of Technology, Sydney.

In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time.
The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call.
To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year.
Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky.
Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated.
A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday).
Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals:
"With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?"
He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt.
Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case.
Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%.
The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions.
Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar.
It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more.
How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street.
Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode."
The "de-rating" and "de-risking" process has surely been notable in recent weeks, with small and cyclical stocks under significant valuation pressure and hedge funds aggressively repositioning out of tech.
Is it enough to enliven buyers into or after the election?
Ned Davis Research thematic strategist Pat Tschosik notes his firm's proprietary market-breadth reading Big Mo Tape tentatively turning higher from oversold readings. "If Big Tech disappoints on Q3 earnings, we may get a full market washout and Big Mo could head even lower like it did in October 2023. Perhaps this is what is needed to set up for a post-midterm-election rally into yearend."
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors sees a similar level to JPMorgan's as the market's breaking point, while evaluating his sentiment indicator.
Kolovos on the latest reading: "A noticeable sentiment reset is underway on the heels of the AI trade unwind and tightening financial conditions.  The good news is that bullish sentiment is finally starting to wash out, which should set the stage for a year-end rally. However, a break below the mid-September lows on the S&P 500 near 7,500 would warn that something more than a routine pullback is unfolding."
-There's something of a paradox at work – or a collective investor blind spot - when the bond market is finally offering relatively safe income after many years of meager yields and yet people continue to rush for the engineered income delivered by options-selling ETFs. This CNBC.com piece offers a thorough, smart rundown of these strategies, complete with warnings of tax pitfalls. This Bloomberg report details a more aggressive approach through funds many investors don't quite understand, while introducing me to the community of self-styled "dividend nomads."
-Anthropic's proposal to place 5% of its equity into a "public benefit fund" to help groups potentially disadvantaged by AI's propagation and Elon Musk's stated offer to give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child via Trump Accounts suggest that anxiety over AI economic disruption is going from simmer to boil.
We can cynically observe that such efforts also hype these companies' world-changing potency, a form of marketing through scare-mongering sheathed in generosity.  But the concern over AI's impact on current worker groups is well-placed, even if ultimately society adapts around step-function technological change. The best hedge against AI-powered capital overtaking labor is arguably to own more capital, whether through the S&P 500 or other vehicles.
Or one could raise the value of one's human capital, through training or becoming excellent at something. This has always been Warren Buffett's answer for how one should become inflation-resistant, as he detailed at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting a few years ago , at the height of the pandemic inflation surge.

The Land of Smiles has become a prime location for Chinese businesses diversifying operations offshore, as Vietnam reaches saturation point
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.
Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.
But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment.

articles.title_orig: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing’s long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
articles.title_zh: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing’s long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration on Tuesday signed off on the Boeing 737 Max 10 after years of delays , a major win for the manufacturer and the last in Boeing's best-selling family of jets to get government approval.
The green light comes weeks after federal officials reviewed a navigation system glitch on the aircraft but deemed it was not a safety-of-flight issue.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's Phil LeBeau that safety is paramount, but he also said the U.S. needs to improve its certification process.
"It takes Boeing, to certify an aircraft in Europe, about half the time, less than half the time that it does in the U.S. You have China now playing to take over in aviation," Duffy said. "We have to certify aircraft more quickly if we're going to compete as Americans."
The 737 Max 10, the largest model in the family that can seat up to 230 people, was set to start flying in 2020, but increased scrutiny following two Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 and other safety issues delayed its certification. Engineering changes were also required, including to an anti-icing system for the aircraft's engines.
Max 10 customers include Alaska Airlines , American Airlines , United Airlines and Delta Air Lines . Boeing said the Max 10 makes up about 30% of its Max backlog.
Airlines can finally start flying passengers soon after planes are certified, but it can take months for carriers to work them into schedules.
"Completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation," Stephanie Pope, CEO of Boeing's commercial airplane unit, said in a news release.
United CEO Scott Kirby told CNBC in August that the airline had been waiting so long for the Max 10 that the lie-flat seats it expected for the plane no longer make sense and are sitting in a warehouse. Alaska Airlines last month said it plans to put lie-flat seats on some of its 737 Max 10s in a push for more premium offerings.
The FAA approved the smallest model of the 737 Max family, the Max 7 , in early August.
Boeing has been working to ramp up production of its 737 Maxes and 787 Dreamliners, which are key to its recovery since airlines and other customers pay the bulk of the aircraft's price upon delivery. The manufacturer opened a fourth production line in Everett, Washington, in July for its 737 Max airplanes.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX quarterly revenue jumps, beats estimates as AI business surges
articles.title_zh: SpaceX quarterly revenue jumps, beats estimates as AI business surges
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares climbed about 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the company reported 161% revenue growth for the third quarter, beating Wall Street estimates, with its artificial intelligence business growing ninefold.
On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla , his automaker, would be a "good idea," adding that the boards of both companies have formed special committees to discuss a tie-up. Tesla reports third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.
Here's how SpaceX did compared to LSEG consensus estimates:
SpaceX said in a release that it recorded operating income of $2.8 billion and net income of $4.4 billion. In the same period a year earlier, SpaceX reported a net loss of $1.05 billion.
CFO Bret Johnsen said on the  call that revenue in the first quarter of 2027 will be $33 billion to $37 billion, trouncing the average $22.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. Johnsen attributed the forecast to "increased visibility into our compute contract pipeline over the next six months."
While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of its Starlink satellite internet service.
Starlink's subscribers base grew to 13.6 million in the quarter, up from 12 million in the prior period.
Total connectivity revenue jumped 69% to $5.25 billion from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Analysts were expecting $4.84 billion, according to StreetAccount. Revenue from consumer Starlink subscribers amounted to $3.12 billion, while the company generated $2.13 billion from government and enterprise customers.
Buzz has been building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation.
SpaceX jumped into AI with the purchase earlier this year of xAI, Musk's AI lab. The company has been rapidly expanding that business by renting out capacity to Google , Anthropic and others.
AI, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," has emerged as its largest business. Revenue jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Analysts expected sales of $6.47 billion, according to StreetAccount.
During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.
Meanwhile, SpaceX's launch business was up just slightly in the quarter, with sales rising to $1.77 billion from $1.67 billion a year ago.
Almost all of SpaceX's profit still comes from Starlink. Operating income in the connectivity unit about doubled to $2.37 billion. The AI business swung to a profit of $431 million, while the space division lost $7 million.
Between infrastructure, cloud deals and paying users of the Grok AI models and products, Musk said on the call that annual recurring revenue by the end of next year will be between $500 billion and $1 trillion. Analysts are projecting full-year 2027 revenue of about $110 billion, according to LSEG, which would be up more than 100% from this year.
What you need to know ahead of the earnings report:
Musk said the boards at Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger "at the request of shareholders," noting that these groups "consist of independent directors."
Because Musk is a "conflicted party," he said he can't be in the discussions.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said, referring to the development of software, chips and more.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this."
Musk said that on the Tesla side, "we will need a 50% vote of all shares -- not just those who vote -- but of all shareholders, and that's quite a high hurdle."
Venture capitalist Ira Ehrenpreis is on the boards of both companies.
Musk said on the call that SpaceX aims to reach "volume production" of AI chips, now in development with partners Tesla and Intel , during the third quarter of 2028 at the Terafab factory that's planned in Texas.
Musk thanked ASML and other suppliers for prioritizing equipment deliveries for the factory.
SpaceX secured significant tax incentives in June for the facility despite local opposition from residents concerned about the strain on local resources.
According to a report from the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday, Musk ordered restrictions on the use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, in Ukraine in recent weeks, impeding some military operations and the country's ability to defend against intensifying attacks by Russia.
Musk previously pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and President Donald Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
The Journal, citing a person familiar with the situation, said Musk talked to senior administration officials, including Trump, "before imposing the new speed cap."
The limits caused Ukraine's drones to lose Starshield connectivity when traveling at speed over 100 miles per hour.
SpaceX said in its shareholder deck that AI growth was spurred by "the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor and increased Grok adoption."
Of its $19.6 billion in capital expenditures in the quarter, more than $16.4 billion was committed to the AI business.
Musk said on the company's call that SpaceX aims to "deploy power, cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than anyone else."
In its Memphis-area data centers, SpaceX's AI business is on track to be able to bring 200,000 of Nvidia's Grace Blackwell system online "every month for the remainder of this year."
SpaceX reported that its Starlink subscriber count rose to 13.6 million in the third quarter, with average revenue per user increasing to $69, up from 12 million Starlink subscribers and ARPU of $66 in the prior period.
The company boasted in an investor update that Starlink was activated in over 3,800 aircraft as of the quarter's end. Customers include American Airlines.
Musk recently threatened Delta CEO Ed Bastian, saying he would lose his job because his airline has not yet made Starlink wireless internet available in their planes.
SpaceX is scheduled to hold its third-quarter earnings call at 4:30 p.m. ET. The company encouraged shareholders to submit questions online ahead of the meeting.
Musk's other public company, Tesla, is scheduled to post third-quarter results on Wednesday. Analysts expect revenue at the electric vehicle maker to dip slightly from a year ago to $27.9 billion, according to LSEG.
Tesla shares are down about 17% this year as of Tuesday, leaving the company with a market cap of almost $1.5 trillion.

SpaceX is relatively new to the cloud computing business. Many of its competitors in the space, the so-called neoclouds, have been getting hammered on Wall Street of late on concerns that rising interest rates are going to make the costly buildout financially burdensome.
CoreWeave and Nebius are down 28% so far in October, while IREN has plunged about 35%. Earlier this month, Australian AI data center operator Firmus withdrew its planned IPO, citing market volatility and conditions.

articles.title_orig: China defends DeepSeek after US ban of its AI from government systems
articles.title_zh: China defends DeepSeek after US ban of its AI from government systems
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG (AP) — China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek's products by federal civilian agencies and warned of retaliatory measures as the two AI powers race to develop the technology.
The Department of Homeland Security said the agencies should remove DeepSeek products as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek from their IT systems, according to a notice made public on Monday.
The latest warnings reflect “the depth of strategic distrust between Beijing and Washington” even as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping work hard to keep their personal relationship “warm and constructive,” said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at Washington-based The Asia Group consultancy.
The Homeland Security order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services.
DeepSeek's open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States , and are mostly free to use.
The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” Concerns include that DeepSeek's servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data, the order says.
Asked in Beijing about the U.S. ban, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies.”
“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security,” she told reporters.
China's Ministry of Commerce also expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” against the U.S.'s move, saying late Tuesday that the U.S. side disregarded the consensus reached between Xi and Trump and ignored the broader landscape of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.
Through discriminatory restrictions under “the guise of national security,” the U.S. is trying to suppress and contain China, the commerce ministry statement said. “China will closely monitor the situation and take all necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up a notification system on national security-related incidents, but they remain at odds on many issues .
AI is expected to be on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet again in mid-November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The two leaders last met in September as Xi made a state visit to Washington .
U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them.
The U.S. also has said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek had engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.
And last week, Beijing rolled out its own proposals to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.

Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude-maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal .
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which includes deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion , up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

articles.title_orig: Report: Microsoft's Project Helix planned for 2028 at $1,200 to $1,800 price
articles.title_zh: Report: Microsoft's Project Helix planned for 2028 at $1,200 to $1,800 price
articles.content_orig:
We haven’t heard many details about Microsoft’s upcoming “Project Helix” gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will “play your Xbox and PC games.” In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with “a next-generation handheld device” planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.
That future console price range is based on what has “internally been projected” at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if “Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost,” the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past .
While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore’s Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn’t as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 .
Fortune also reports that Microsoft is beset by internal clashes over whether its upcoming Helix handheld will run a “trimmed-down version of Windows Home”—akin to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally —or a bespoke operating system built and controlled by the Xbox group. Fortune cites “people briefed on the clash” in reporting that one high-level executive threatened to cancel the handheld altogether if they were forced to use Windows.
That threat seemingly helped lead to the current situation with the Xbox team “now largely controlling the direction of the operating system for the project, Fortune writes, though Sharma said the two groups are still working closely together. Fortune also reports that Microsoft has pressured the hardware team to move up the timelines for Project Helix hardware “by at least several months,” in part by using AI tools where applicable.
The profile also cites “people familiar with the strategy” in reporting that Xbox Game Pass will soon shift to a heavily tiered “a la carte” structure that lets subscribers pick and choose “add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer.” That would be an interesting shift from the current Game Pass plans, which all include some level of cloud-based gaming, console exclusives, and console multiplayer even for players who don’t make use of them.
Elsewhere in the wide-ranging profile, Fortune addresses concerns from “several current and former staff members” that Sharma was put in place merely to enact painful cuts before an impending sale of a spinoff of the Xbox group. But the piece also quotes Microsoft executive Judson Althoff pushing back against that idea, saying, “We would not have put [Sharma] on a business we intend to sell. There’s going to be a ton of speculation about all this. Time will tell.”

articles.title_orig: Utah sues Kalshi, saying it’s ‘the manager of a back-alley gambling den’
articles.title_zh: Utah sues Kalshi, saying it’s ‘the manager of a back-alley gambling den’
articles.content_orig:
(Erin Hooley | AP) An ad for the prediction market app Kalshi is displayed on a mobile phone. Utah is suing the company.
Utah is suing Kalshi for what the state calls a “brazen pattern of unlawful conduct,” and is asking a judge to order the company to stop offering wagers in the state and approve a geolocator tool to enforce the ban.
It also wants the prediction market platform, used primarily for sports betting, to pay the millions it has made through fees from wagers Utahns placed and that residents have lost through those bets.
Attorney General Derek Brown stressed that the lawsuit isn’t targeting the more than 32,000 Utahns who have verified Kalshi accounts.
“Let me be clear: It’s against the companies,” Brown said. “It’s not against you.”
Gambling is illegal in Utah as part of the state’s constitution — and Kalshi is “well aware” of that, the complaint filed Tuesday in state court says. It names Kalshi, four of its subsidiaries and two Pennsylvania-based trading companies that provide pricing and liquidity for the platform.
Utah’s prohibition hasn’t stopped gambling companies from operating in what they consider a legal gray area. Kalshi and other prediction markets claim event contracts are financial “swaps” sanctioned by a federal trading commission.
But Kalshi functions the same way as “the manager of a back-alley gambling den,” the state argues, because the company acts as the market maker on its platform, facilitates bets and retains a portion of each bet as its own payment.
The company even has an entity responsible for finalizing and settling wagers, including making payouts, something the state argues means it isn’t just a third-party trading platform.
“It is administering a closed-loop wagering system,” the complaint reads, “where it creates the games, handles the bets, and pays out the winners.”
Attorneys representing Kalshi in a federal lawsuit against the state did not immediately respond to a Tuesday request for comment. Company spokespeople have previously referred to similar lawsuits as a type of “political theater” and said states “can’t just shut down a federally licensed exchange.”
While the state is focused on Kalshi for now, Brown asked other companies using similar means to “follow Utah law.”
(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, shown in 2025, calls on Kalshi and other prediction markets to follow the state's laws.
At first, the complaint says, Kalshi only offered “wagers tied to traditional financial instruments.” But as early as 2024, any attempted distinction between what it does and gambling “collapsed,” the complaint adds, once it started offering sports trading and started using language specifically referring to betting on professional football and other sports.
Kalshi now offers “numerous” types of wagers, which the company refers to as event contracts, the complaint says, and is “regularly” adding more.
It offered as many as 100,000 to 300,000 open wagers, which it calls markets, per day in three months over the summer, according to the complaint.
The event contracts or wagers, the state argues, are “indistinguishable from the format of bets offered through any sportsbook,” including proposition bets, parlays and betting on the point spreads in games.
Kalshi offers more than just sports betting. The complaint spells out various other kinds of wagers people can make, including:
• Elections with wagers like “Blue wave this year?” and “Closest Senate race this year?”
• Politics with options including “[President Donald] Trump’s approval rating Friday” and “Who will be arrested this year?”
• Culture wagers over things like who will headline Coachella in 2027 and the next James Bond.
• Mentions with wagers like whether Trump will mention Arizona at an investment announcement.
The state estimates Kalshi has made between $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees from wagers placed by Utah accounts through the fees it retains as a portion of each wager and that Utahns have lost $5.5 million in individual wagers.
Brown called those “general numbers” and said the state will learn more as it gathers information leading up to a possible civil trial. If Utah succeeds in getting restitution, he said, there isn’t a plan yet for spending that money.
The state is concerned about the “significant and substantial ongoing harm to a significant number of Utahns,” Brown said, and that is why it filed the lawsuit in 3rd District Court.
He had a message for the young men who are the “targets of these online trading apps” about Kalshi and similar companies.
“They’re not your friends. They’re not helping you invest. They’re not providing you with insight or opportunity,” Brown said. “Frankly, they are engineered to do one thing and one thing alone, and that is empty your wallet.”
He urged people who are losing money to stop and seek help through the National Problem Gambling Helpline by calling or texting 1-800-697-3738 or visiting 1800myreset.org .
The lawsuit follows a legal dispute with Kalshi, which tried to settle the legal question earlier this year when it preemptively sued Utah, alleging the federal government’s Commodity Futures Trading Commission has authority over the markets Kalshi runs.
In August, a federal judge sided with the state in its case against Kalshi, further advancing Utah’s ability to regulate prediction markets in the state.
Kalshi appealed that decision to the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and sought to block enforcement of Utah’s laws during the appeal. The court denied that order last month, and the appeal is still pending.
Utah is not the only state battling Kalshi.
Red and blue states alike have sued to take on the company and other prediction markets. Several are locked in litigation over whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling regulations.
In July, Brown joined 43 other attorneys general in signing a letter attacking the platforms as a “new form of casino” that companies use to “manipulate others” — namely young people who are “particularly vulnerable.”

The tanker "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems," the statement added.
Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.

articles.title_orig: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings preview: flat revenue, falling profits
articles.title_zh: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings preview: flat revenue, falling profits
articles.content_orig:
Tesla reports its third-quarter 2026 financial results tomorrow, October 21, after the market closes. The earnings call follows at 5:30 p.m. ET.
Wall Street expects revenue to come in flat and earnings per share to drop 10% from a year ago, even though Tesla just beat its own delivery consensus by more than 24,000 vehicles.
We already have the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3 , down 2.1% from its all-time record of 497,099 in Q3 2025, but well above the 461,974 consensus Tesla compiled from 24 analysts.
It built only 464,391 vehicles during the quarter. So Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it produced, the second quarter in a row it has worked down inventory after building roughly 50,000 excess vehicles in Q1.
It’s still a two-car company. Model 3 and Model Y made up 478,237 of those deliveries, while “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi and what’s left of Model S and X) fell 48% year-over-year to 8,295 units.
Energy storage was the weak spot. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh, up 9.6% from 12.5 GWh a year ago, but well short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected and below the 14.2 GWh record it set in Q4 2025.
The Wall Street consensus calls for $28.06 billion in revenue, with the Estimize crowd a bit more bullish at $28.36 billion. Either way, that’s flat against the $28.1 billion Tesla reported in Q3 2025. Wall Street estimates range from $25.1 billion to $30.6 billion.
Flat isn’t as bad as it sounds. Q3 2025 was inflated by US buyers rushing to grab the $7,500 federal tax credit before it expired on September 30, 2025, so matching it without the credit would be a decent result.
But look at the sequential picture. Tesla posted $28.24 billion in revenue in Q2 2026 on 480,126 deliveries and 13.5 GWh of storage. Q3 had more of both, yet Wall Street is modeling slightly less revenue and Estimize only about $120 million more, which means both are baking in lower average selling prices.
Analysts expect non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.45, down 10% from $0.50 in Q3 2025. The Estimize consensus is a little higher at $0.48, and Wall Street estimates range from $0.30 to $0.70.
Take that number with a grain of salt. In Q2, Tesla came in at $0.33 against a $0.53 consensus, as its operating margin collapsed to 1.4% . Operating income fell 57% to $398 million while operating expenses jumped 47% to $4.35 billion.
Tesla has now missed the Street’s EPS estimate in two of the last four quarters. And its EPS has declined year-over-year in five of the last seven.
The number we’ll be watching first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits. It dropped to 16.3% in Q2 from 19.2% in Q1, which Tesla blamed on a $230 million warranty true-down and tariff relief that helped Q1 and didn’t repeat.
Regulatory credits won’t bail it out either. They brought in only $146 million in Q2, down 67% from a year earlier, and that pure-profit revenue keeps shrinking now that automakers no longer face federal CAFE penalties.
Then there’s cash. Tesla burned $1.09 billion in free cash flow in Q2 as capital expenditures more than doubled to $5.8 billion, and management guided to more than $25 billion in capex for 2026, with spending weighted to the second half. Another negative free cash flow quarter wouldn’t be a surprise.
Energy is worth a look too. The storage business ran a 20.4% gross margin in Q2, and Tesla says it expects the low-to-mid 20% range long term. With Q3 deployments missing estimates by more than 2 GWh, energy won’t offset much.
Tesla’s Say Technologies Q&A for the call closes today at 4 p.m. ET. It drew 832 questions from about 2,860 participants representing 3.85 million shares.
That’s more people than last quarter (about 1,710) but less than half the shares, which were 8.6 million in Q2.
Here are the top questions ranked by shares represented:
The auto business is flat. Deliveries are up 8.8% year-to-date at 1,324,681, which is a real recovery from two years of decline, but Q3 came in below last year and Tesla still sells almost nothing outside of Model 3 and Model Y.
"And shareholders mostly don’t care."
And the ones that do (such as myself) have sold their shares years ago after Musk lost his mind and got involved in politics and other bad decisions.
So the quarter comes down to margins and spending. If auto margins ex-credits hold around 16% and opex stops climbing 40%+ a year, the Q2 miss was a one-off. If not, Tesla is spending more than $25 billion this year on AI, Optimus, Cybercab and chips while its core business barely breaks even at the operating level. That’s a car company funding a very expensive bet out of a shrinking profit pool.
And shareholders mostly don’t care. Look at the questions: Cybercab, FSD, Optimus, HW3. The top question about Tesla’s consumer lineup was a request for a van.
They are completely delusional, waiting for questionable new products to bring in money while watching their cash cows stop growing, something that was completely avoidable if Musk hadn’t bet the whole company on autonomy too early.

articles.title_zh: EU rejects Turkish-Libyan maritime agreement as ‘invalid and void’
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has strongly criticized the eastern Libyan parliament’s ratification on Tuesday of Libya’s maritime memorandum with Turkey, reiterating that the agreement violates the sovereign rights of third countries and does not comply with the Law of the Sea.
The EU stressed that its position, established by the European Council in 2019, remains unchanged, describing the agreement as “invalid and void”. It also reaffirmed its solidarity with Greece and Cyprus and reiterated its opposition to any external intervention in Libya.
In a joint statement, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and the President of the European Council Antonio Costa noted: “We deeply regret the ratification today by the Libyan Parliament of the so-called Libyan-Türkiye Memorandum of Understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdictions in the Mediterranean Sea.”
“We recall that the EU’s position on this matter was clearly stated by the European Council in 2019 and remains unchanged,” it said adding:
“This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void. We reaffirm our solidarity with Greece and Cyprus. We reiterate the EU’s well known position against any outside interference in Libya.”
Libya’s eastern parliament backed the maritime agreement with Turkey on Tuesday, reviving a deal that Athens has long opposed.
Control of Libya ​is split between rival western and eastern administrations, ​with the east under military commander Khalifa Haftar.
The maritime deal covering claims in the eastern Mediterranean had been agreed with Turkey in 2019 by the internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA) in ​the west, but ​was rejected by authorities in eastern Libya, sparking a ​boycott, and in Egypt and Greece.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.title_zh: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed the visit in comments to reporters Tuesday, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.
Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections .
Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying , "it is not convenient for us."
Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday , calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."

articles.title_orig: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
articles.title_zh: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
articles.content_orig:
Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn’t available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature.
As Google points out , a generative AI’s outputs are better “when it knows the world and knows you,” which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don’t have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar.
Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, “Google built-in” is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it’s the other way around.
Google says Personal Intelligence is a natural fit for the car, allowing you to focus on the road instead of providing detailed instructions to your digital assistant. For example, you can say “take me to my doctor’s appointment,” and Gemini can get that data from your connected calendar. It can also leverage visual analysis to find locations in your photos to begin navigation.
Personal Intelligence is off by default, but it’s possible you’ve turned it on at some point while interacting with Gemini, which has now replaced Assistant on all devices. Google has a habit of nudging users to opt in to data sharing in Gemini, so you may not even realize you’re sharing account data with Gemini, and those settings will transfer over to Android Auto. For Google built-in vehicles, you only get personal results if you’ve connected a device over Bluetooth. You will be able to turn this off via in-car settings even if your phone has Personal Intelligence enabled.
There may be other people interacting with the screen in your car, so perhaps you don’t want more of your account data informing replies. The Personal Intelligence options are just one level deep in the Gemini app’s settings. You’re looking for the “Connected Apps” section, where you can toggle Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, etc.), Search, Photos, and more.
While Google says it doesn’t use your personal data to train Gemini, it does use your inputs and outputs while using the AI. Some of those outputs can have personal information when you have these services connected, and while the company does attempt to filter that out, it won’t make any promises . The rollout of Personal Intelligence in your car is probably a good opportunity to check your data-sharing settings and make sure you’re comfortable with them.

Surprise! Hot on the heels of PlayStation's own upscaling tech announcements, Microsoft and AMD just revealed that the firm's flagship FSR 4.1 tech is coming to the Xbox platform.
FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) is a technology from AMD that renders games at a lower resolution, and then uses machine learning to generate a sharper image. Since the hardware isn't working as hard, that overhead can be used for performance.
FSR 4.1 is a big leap over previous versions, and Microsoft has partnered with AMD to bring it not only to Xbox Series X , but also Xbox Ally X , Xbox Ally S and Xbox Series S — the latter two of which should benefit from very, very big performance boosts as a result.
"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are, and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet explained. From the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds, to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and AutoSR that helps developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players."
"Today, we're excited to take another step forward together. With FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox. Now, we've worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players. Now, whether you're playing on an Xbox Ally handheld, as well as coming soon to Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
It's unclear exactly when these technologies will roll out to Xbox devices. It sounds as though FSR 4.1 will hit Xbox Ally X before the year end, but Xbox Series X|S are listed as "coming soon," with no exact window offered.
Sadly, it seems the Xbox Ally base model is fully incompatible with FSR 4.1, which is a bit of a shame, but it should prove transformative for those with the Xbox Ally X and the just-released Xbox Ally X20 , as well as the Xbox Series S.

The Xbox Series S has historically been difficult for developers owing to its irregular RAM allocation, but if FSR 4.1 can do some of the heavy lifting, it should ease the pressure on developers to deliver a native 1080p image.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations about withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations about withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war . Washington’s backing is in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”
Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo, and Kushner joined the talks remotely. Zelenskyy also held talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb before he met the U.S. delegation.
Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication of what that might be.
Trump has waived sanctions and agreed on a diesel deal with Russia, apparently in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate” in his latest rebuke.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years, that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters Monday. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Tuesday: “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office.”
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles Sunday for the third time in recent days.
In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.
Zelenskyy said early Tuesday that he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Zelenskyy said later Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice. The change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including the phone call with Rubio earlier in the day, he said.
Rubio told reporters that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing in U.S. support for Ukraine had changed.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he said at the start of a trip to India.
When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said, the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he said. “We have our own needs, too.”
Ukrainian officials, including Zelenskyy, have made it clear that they accuse the U.S. of imposing restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks deadlier.
“That’s scandalous. That’s outrageous. That’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.
Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a 1-year-old girl who they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“ The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
articles.title_zh: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
articles.content_orig:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.
As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.
The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here – Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.
“This will be a massive cleanup job, bigger than Heartbleed,” Filippo Valsorda, a cryptography engineer and a cryptography maintainer for the open source Go programming language, told Ars. “There will be a very, very long tail, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, unmaintained CLI tools that shipped their own copy of the roots (which is common in some ecosystems, like Python). Also, Linux distributions are still rolling out updates, some of them are not ready yet, and then system administrators will need to apply them to a lot of machines.”
Heartbleed is the name of a critical vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptography library. In 2014, it came under mass exploitation . Exploits let many unaffiliated hackers decrypt TLS-protected exchanges between parties. They also recovered private TLS certificate keys, session cookies, and passwords. The attacks compromised thousands of servers, some belonging to large companies and government agencies around the world.
Recovery required a long series of steps that took years. Steps included patching OpenSSL on all affected devices, reissuing millions of TLS keys, revoking old certificates, rotating passwords and session tokens and updating embedded devices and other forgotten systems—something that was extremely time- and resource-intensive, especially at Internet scale.
“Every time you need a lot of different people in different contexts to do something, it will take a long time,” Valsorda explained. “This time it’s worse because there’s more contexts, more people, and more heterogeneity.”
The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2 384 , or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.
“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”
Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”
At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.
As noted, most browsers have already blocked the intermediate certificates. The exception appears to be Edge running on Windows 10, which at the time this article went live was still connecting to 12 vulnerable hosts. In response to questions asking why and if the company has plans to do so, a Microsoft representative the company will be in touch if it has anything to “share.” Meanwhile, Signal, WhatsApp, Wireguard, and other apps that don’t rely on TLS for confidentiality aren’t affected. This page and the emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com site show apps known to be patched so far.
The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.
One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network—at a coffee shop, university, or other organization—face much less of a challenge.

articles.title_zh: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.
A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.
Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.
District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".
"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.
The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.
In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.
However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.
The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.
The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".
Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.

articles.title_zh: PHP RCE Zero-Days CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 Leak Early
articles.content_orig:

PHP will ship fixes for two leaked critical flaws rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 on October 21 at 14:00 UTC, a day before the embargo was set to lift.
Sulochana is a staff writer and technology contributor at Cyber Kendra, covering the latest tech news, cybersecurity, and digital insights.
The PHP security team said on Tuesday that it will ship a security release on Wednesday, October 21, to fix two critical vulnerabilities, after information about the embargoed flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, leaked online.
In an advance notice on php.net, the team said the release is scheduled for 14:00 UTC, which is 10:00 a.m. ET and 19:30 IST. It rated both vulnerabilities 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and urged all PHP users to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the builds are available. The PHP Foundation shared the same notice on X.
The PHP team said full details, affected versions, and fixed versions will be published with the release. It also said it may ship earlier if details of either flaw become public or if evidence of active exploitation emerges.
Wednesday is a day earlier than the date researchers under embargo had been working to. Security firm watchTowr said everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday at 11:00 a.m. ET, and the first public report of the leak pointed to October 22.
That report came in a “Tell HN” post on Hacker News at 15:20 UTC on October 20. Citing a “reliable source”, user petecooper wrote that two PHP remote code execution flaws rated CVSS 10.0 were due for disclosure, affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. The poster admitted having no evidence, and the post was later flagged, but screenshots were already circulating on X and Mastodon.
watchTowr then confirmed the leak, saying the information concerned zero-day RCE vulnerabilities in PHP. “We can confirm that they’re real,” the company said, adding that it could not share more and urging administrators to patch once fixes are out.
We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real. CVE-2926-109618/619 We cannot share further information right now. Take this seriously and apply patches when available. pic.twitter.com/kguM8fpq13
Security researcher Florian Roth wrote on X that the flaw is an RCE in PHP core and that only PHP 8 will receive patches. PHP 5 and PHP 7 reached end of life years ago, so servers still running them would stay exposed without an official fix. Nicolas Krassas said he will publish a hands-on lab once the embargo lifts, and Kevin Beaumont flagged the leak on Mastodon .
The official severity differs from the leak. PHP rates both bugs 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, while the leaked posts cited 10.0 and did not say which version of the scoring system they used. The PHP notice does not name the CVE IDs or describe the bugs as code execution flaws; those details come from watchTowr and the leaked reports.
No technical details have been made public. Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 remain in reserved status, and none of the posts identify the affected function, extension, or configuration. In an FAQ on the flaws , watchTowr said it had seen no exploitation in the wild, that the bugs are not in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no workaround exists before the patch.
An embargo is a private window during which a vendor coordinates fixes with Linux distributions, hosting providers, and security firms, so that patched builds ship at the same moment as the advisory. Once the severity and date leaked, anyone already holding the bugs knew how long they had before fixes landed.

articles.title_orig: Dear Tim Sweeney, You Could Learn A Thing Or Two From The Xbox Exec Who Posted So Bad That He Had To Delete His Account
articles.title_zh: Dear Tim Sweeney, You Could Learn A Thing Or Two From The Xbox Exec Who Posted So Bad That He Had To Delete His Account
articles.content_orig:
A better world is possible
In the relatively short time since we launched Aftermath, we’ve watched the world change markedly as generative AI and authoritarianism have reshaped a landscape that was already full of fissures. Through it all, we have held firm in one core value: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney should log off .
I bring this up because now we’ve even found him a potential role model: Xbox senior business strategy manager Brandon Stirrup. We’re talking about a man molded in Sweeney’s own image—at least, as far as posting goes—but with one crucial distinction: Stirrup ultimately logged off.
He began his posting spree over the weekend, boasting that he’d "vibe coded a bad but improvable game" and that “anyone can build a game.” This gave way to multiple diatribes about how generative AI is the de facto future of game development.
"Look if I'm fired tomorrow it will be because I told you the truth that nobody wants you to know,” he wrote on Sunday. “You can make a game with a simple prompt and yes you can make custom, tailored games. Everything you want in a game is right there for the taking, for better or worse. … I’m happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they’re not using AI. It’s time to accept and move forward.”
Never mind that it is extremely well known that some developers who work at Microsoft-owned studios are using AI. Going into Monday, Stirrup still had more golden wisdom to share. He tweeted:
Then, yesterday evening, something resembling common sense stirred up in Stirrup, and he deleted his Twitter account. An Xbox source told PC Gamer he did so because of “the volume of replies he was receiving.”
This, to me, is the platonic ideal of a Bad Poster, the example all others should follow. You say some dumb bullshit, dig your heels in for a while, get absolutely obliterated in the replies, and then delete your account. Stirrup even did us a favor by speedrunning the whole process. Fantastic. No notes.
Tim Sweeney, I’m begging you: learn from this. You’re never gonna beat Stirrup’s time, but you can still log off whenever you want. I guarantee it’ll be better than the elaborate series of humiliation rituals that has become your life.
